Interior environmental wide of one of the old German caravans visible in the supplied campsite reference image. It must clearly feel like the interior of that same modest, slightly weathered late-20th-century caravan parked on the damp Baltic campsite outside: faded beige and brown plastic laminate, aging cream-colored wall panels, cheap veneered cabinetry, worn upholstery, small caravan windows, thin curtains, a narrow built-in table, an old gas cooker, tiny sink, storage compartments and traces of condensation around the window frames. 35mm lens at approximately T4, camera positioned just inside the caravan entrance at natural standing eye level, looking lengthwise through the interior. Wide enough to establish the space but not an exaggerated ultra-wide lens. Straight, restrained perspective, realistic optical geometry in the immediate foreground.
The caravan belongs to a man who has been alive for thousands of years.
At first glance the room appears believable: cramped, domestic, slightly messy, inhabited by someone who has been living here for a long time. But the longer the viewer looks, the more strange details appear. Objects from completely incompatible periods of human history coexist naturally among ordinary campsite belongings, as though their owner simply accumulated them personally and stopped caring how bizarre the collection looks.
The objects are not displayed like a museum and are not arranged for the camera. They are casually integrated into everyday life.
On the table beside a half-empty coffee mug and an overflowing ashtray lies a genuinely ancient hand-hammered coin, darkened by centuries of handling. A Roman-era bronze fibula is casually used as a paperweight on a stack of modern electricity bills. Several brittle handwritten letters on uneven old paper are pushed underneath a cheap plastic lighter. A small medieval devotional object sits beside a packet of cigarettes. A tarnished maritime compass from the age of sail hangs from a hook normally intended for kitchen towels. A scratched 19th-century pocket watch lies open beside a modern digital alarm clock. An extremely old hand-drawn coastal map with faded ink has been folded and unfolded so many times that the edges are almost destroyed.
There are small personal remnants from many different centuries rather than obvious famous historical treasures: fragments of handwriting in different alphabets, worn coins, old seals, a primitive iron key, a tiny carved bone object, a faded daguerreotype portrait, a cracked porcelain figurine, an old brass telescope, a wooden box darkened by centuries of touch, photographs from different decades, stacks of postcards, obsolete cigarette packages, forgotten currencies, a cheap 1980s cassette player, VHS tapes, an early mobile phone and contemporary objects all mixed together.
Nothing should look newly bought from an antique shop. Every old object has genuine age: oxidized metal, fingerprints, worn edges, faded pigments, tiny repairs, dirt embedded in crevices. Some pieces appear almost worthless, yet have obviously been kept for centuries because they meant something to him.
Avoid making the caravan excessively cluttered. There should still be negative space and readable composition. The collection feels accumulated rather than decorated.
The most important element is the architecture of the interior.
Something is subtly impossible about the size of the caravan.
The entrance and immediate foreground retain the believable dimensions of the small caravan visible outside, but deeper into the frame the room refuses to resolve into a measurable space. A narrow passage between cupboards appears to continue several meters farther than the exterior dimensions could physically allow. Shelves disappear gradually into darkness. Another section of wall seems to exist behind a corner where logically there should only be the outside of the caravan.
Do not portray this as obvious fantasy architecture.
There are no floating objects, portals, glowing magic, warped walls or dramatic visual effects.
Instead create an almost subconscious spatial contradiction: every individual architectural element looks completely normal, yet their combined depth cannot be understood.
The viewer should repeatedly attempt to determine where the rear wall is and fail.
One small doorway or curtain toward the rear appears to lead into another dim section of the caravan, but its destination remains completely obscured. Beyond it, perhaps another faint tungsten practical can be seen much farther away than should physically be possible.
A narrow mirror reflects part of the room, but the reflected perspective reveals slightly more interior depth than should exist. The effect must be subtle enough that the viewer may initially question whether they imagined it.
Furniture overlaps sightlines. Hanging coats, shelving, partially open cupboards, curtains and deep shadow constantly block any clean view through the entire room. No single line of sight reveals the full interior.
The space should feel as though the caravan has no clearly definable end.
It is not enormous like a palace and never becomes a fantasy warehouse. Instead it feels intimate and claustrophobic while simultaneously suggesting potentially endless hidden depth.
This contradiction is essential.
The immortal has lived so long that the caravan itself now feels like a physical manifestation of his memory: countless periods of history layered into a space that cannot be taken in all at once.
Keep the supernatural quality ambiguous. It should never be clear whether the caravan is actually impossible, whether perspective is deceiving us, or whether the darkness simply hides more than expected.

[SHOT] Environmental establishing shot of an aging provincial German football stadium near the Baltic coast, somewhere between a forgotten regional-league ground and an oversized municipal sports complex built decades ago. The architecture feels unmistakably Central European and slightly post-industrial: long weathered concrete terraces, rows of dark wet seating, narrow steel handrails, chain-link fencing, old blue-painted barriers with chipped paint, a simple covered grandstand with a heavy corrugated-metal roof, exposed concrete support structure, and tall skeletal floodlight towers rising into a pale overcast sky.
A reddish-brown running track separates the stands from the football pitch. The grass is maintained but imperfect, deep muted green with worn areas near the touchline. Simple dugouts, maintenance gates and utilitarian service structures sit around the edge of the field. No modern LED architecture, no luxury boxes, no polished Bundesliga atmosphere. This is a stadium that has hosted thousands of ordinary Saturday matches, youth tournaments, local derbies and rainy winter fixtures.
The stands are almost completely empty. Evidence of people remains: crushed paper cups, cigarette packets, wet newspapers, plastic food trays, discarded tickets and a few empty beer bottles scattered between the concrete steps. Nothing arranged decoratively; the debris should feel accidental and mundane. Rust stains run beneath bolts and railings. Moss and dark moisture collect in cracks. Paint has faded unevenly after years of Baltic rain, salt air and cold winters.
The stadium should feel strangely too large for the small town surrounding it, as though its best years happened decades ago. Beyond the far stand: fragments of modest residential roofs, industrial sheds, bare trees, utility poles and flat northern-German landscape disappearing beneath a gray horizon. No recognizable club branding, no real sponsors, no readable corporate logos, no famous stadium identifiers.
It is early morning after rain. The concrete is still wet, reflecting small patches of the washed-out sky. Cold diffused daylight, no direct sun. Thin atmospheric moisture in the distance, but absolutely no cinematic fog machine effect. The air should almost feel cold when looking at the image.
Composition inspired by documentary photographs of old European football grounds: camera positioned high on one side of the terraces, looking diagonally across the empty stands toward the pitch so that railings, concrete steps and the roof structure create strong foreground layers. Let the grandstand occupy a substantial part of the frame rather than presenting a symmetrical postcard view. The football pitch appears partially rather than perfectly centered. Include foreground obstruction from railings or structural elements to make the camera feel physically present inside the stadium.
35mm Zeiss Super Speed Mk II, T4. Deep enough focus that the architecture, opposite stand and floodlight towers remain clearly readable while maintaining natural optical depth. Locked-off observational frame with barely perceptible human camera breathing. No dramatic hero composition. No characters posing in the frame. The place itself is the protagonist.
The emotional quality is not “abandoned stadium” horror. It is ordinary, tired, melancholy provincial life: functional, slightly neglected, damp and deeply familiar. A place that is still used, just currently empty. Northern European realism with a subtle sense that something important is about to happen in an otherwise completely unimportant place.

soft shadows,
